(i) - (a), (ii) - (b), and (iii) - (c) (i) - (b), (ii) - (a), and (iii) - (c) (i) - (b), (ii) - (c), and (iii) - (a) (i) - (a), (ii) - (c), and (iii) - (b)
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the two lists List I and List II given below:

\[
\begin{array}{|l|l|}
\hline \textbf{List I} & \textbf{List II} \\
\hline \text{Context-free languages} & \text{Closed under union} \\
\hline \text{Recursive languages} & \text{Not closed under complementation} \\
\hline \text{Regular languages} & \text{Closed under intersection} \\
\hline
\end{array}
\]

For matching of items in List I with those in List II, which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?

  1. (i) - (a), (ii) - (b), and (iii) - (c)
  2. (i) - (b), (ii) - (a), and (iii) - (c)
  3. (i) - (b), (ii) - (c), and (iii) - (a)
  4. (i) - (a), (ii) - (c), and (iii) - (b)
questions.explanation: CFL languages are closed under all operations except complement, intersection, and difference.  Recursive languages are not closed under substitution and homomorphism.  Regular languages are closed under all operations. So option $(B, C)$ is correct. for more:  Closure Property of Language Families

questions.questionHtml:
A regular language $L$ is accepted by a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with $n$ states. Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE?

  1. $L$ may have an accepting NFA with $< n$ states.
  2. $L$ may have an accepting DFA with $<n$ states.
  3. There exists a DFA with $\leq 2^{n}$ states that accepts $L$.
  4. Every DFA that accepts $L$ has $>2^{n}$ states.

options.label: A
options.text: $L$ may have an accepting NFA with $< n$ states.

options.label: B
options.text: $L$ may have an accepting DFA with $<n$ states.

options.label: C
options.text: There exists a DFA with $\leq 2^{n}$ states that accepts $L$.

options.label: D
options.text: Every DFA that accepts $L$ has $>2^{n}$ states.

questions.explanation: Given that L accepted by a non-deterministic finite automata with 'n' states. Option A: L may have an accepting NFA with < n states. Please note that it is saying that L may have. If our original NFA having redundant states, then we may have a NFA with less than 'n' states. Hence, this option is correct. Option B. L may have an accepting DFA with < n states. Please note that it is saying that L may have. If our original NFA having redundant states, then we may have a NFA which is same as DFA with less than 'n' states. Hence, this option is correct. Option c. There exists a DFA with ≤ 2" states that accepts L. if NFA have 'n' states, then equivalent DFA may have maximum $2^{N}$ states. Hence, this option is correct. https://gateoverflow.in/3266/gate-it-2008-question-6 https://gateoverflow.in/204080/gate-cse-2018-question-6 Option D: Every DFA that accepts L has > 2" states. As option B is true, this must be false.

questions.questionText: Consider the following two languages over the alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$, where $m$ and $n$ are natural numbers. $$\begin{aligned} L_{1} & =\left\{a^{m} b^{m} c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1\right\} \\ L_{2} & =\left\{a^{m} b^{n} c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1\right\} \end{aligned}$$ Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT? Both $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are context-free languages. $L_{1}$ is a context-free language but $L_{2}$ is not a context-free language. $L_{1}$ is not a context-free language but $L_{2}$ is a context-free language. Neither $L_{1}$ nor $L_{2}$ are context-free languages.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following two languages over the alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$, where $m$ and $n$ are natural numbers.

$$\begin{aligned} L_{1} & =\left\{a^{m} b^{m} c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1\right\} \\ L_{2} & =\left\{a^{m} b^{n} c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1\right\} \end{aligned}$$

Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT?

  1. Both $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are context-free languages.
  2. $L_{1}$ is a context-free language but $L_{2}$ is not a context-free language.
  3. $L_{1}$ is not a context-free language but $L_{2}$ is a context-free language.
  4. Neither $L_{1}$ nor $L_{2}$ are context-free languages.

options.label: B
options.text: $L_{1}$ is a context-free language but $L_{2}$ is not a context-free language.

options.label: C
options.text: $L_{1}$ is not a context-free language but $L_{2}$ is a context-free language.

questions.explanation: Given: $L1=\{  a^m b^m c^{m+n}  ∣  m,n≥1  \}$ We can write this as: $L1 = \{  a^m b^m c^m⋅c^n  ∣  m,n≥1 \} = \{ a^m b^m c^m c^+ \} $  $L1 =\{ a^m b^m c^m c^+ \}$ So this seems like: $a^m b^m c^m$ followed by at least one more $c$ The language ${ a^m b^m c^m }$ is not context-free .It is a classic example of a language that is not context-free , because if we push $a$ ,pop $b$ then there will be no element for $c$ to be compared. Now for  $L2 = \{a^m b^n c^{m+n} ∣ m,n≥1\}$ For this language we can push $a,b$ then pop $c.$ Therefore, L1 is not Context free but L2 is context free Answer : $C$ Tejaswee_Bommaluleni answered Jul 9, 2025 • edited Jan 17 by Umesh Shelke Tejaswee_Bommaluleni comment Share Follow See all 3 Comments 3 3 Comments reply msrsaditya commented Aug 9, 2025 reply Follow flag if there's a^nb^nc^2n then it's not CFL because we're not checking # a's and # b's but if there's a^mb^nc^m+n t

questions.questionText: Let L1 is Regular Language and Ls is Context Free Language, Then how to solve :  L1​∪(L2​∪L2'​​)   Means should we have to do :  (1)  (L2​∪L2'​​)  : CFL U CFL' = Universal Language (because L U L' = Universal Language) or (2)  (L2​∪L2'​​) : CFL U CFL' = CFL U CSL = CSL   Because if we use 1 then final answer will be Universal Language (i.e. Regular Language) and if we use 2 the final answer will be Context Sensitive Language
questions.questionHtml:
Let L1 is Regular Language and Ls is Context Free Language,

Then how to solve : L1​∪(L2​∪L2'​​) 
Means should we have to do : 
(1) (L2​∪L2'​​) : CFL U CFL' = Universal Language (because L U L' = Universal Language) or
(2) (L2​∪L2'​​) : CFL U CFL' = CFL U CSL = CSL 

Because if we use 1 then final answer will be Universal Language (i.e. Regular Language) and if we use 2 the final answer will be Context Sensitive Language
questions.explanation: Your both answer are correct as CFL will also be CSL but whenever you can get closer to lower language try to do so. As it will result in more generalised answer

questions.questionText: Fix $0<\lambda<1$. Choose $\epsilon>0$ such that $\epsilon+\frac{\lambda^{2}}{4} \leq \frac{\lambda}{2}$. Consider the metric space \[ X:=\left\{\psi \in \mathcal{C}^{1}([-\epsilon, \epsilon]):|y+\psi(y)| \leq \frac{\lambda}{2} \text { for all } y \in[-\epsilon, \epsilon]\right\} \] with the induced supremum metric from $\mathcal{C}^{1}([-\epsilon, \epsilon])$, which we denote by $d$. (Recall: $\mathcal{C}^{1}([-\epsilon, \epsilon])$ is the set of real-valued differentiable functions on $[-\epsilon, \epsilon]$ whose derivative is continuous.) Show that there is a function $A: X \longrightarrow X$ given by \[ (A \psi)(y)=-(y+\psi(y))^{2} \] Show that if $\psi \in X$ is such that $A \psi=\psi$, then the function $x=y+\psi(y)$ is an inverse to the function $y=x+x^{2}$, locally near the origin. In the next few steps, we show that such a $\psi$ exists. Show that $d\left(A \psi_{1}, A \psi_{2}\right) \leq \lambda d\left(\psi_{1}, \psi_{2}\right)$. Let $\phi \in X$. Show that the sequence $A^{n} \phi, n \geq 1$ is a Cauchy sequence, and it has a limit. By $A^{n}$, we mean the $n$-fold composition $A \circ A \circ \cdots \circ A$. (You may use the fact that $X$ is complete with respect to d.) Show that there exists $\psi \in X$ such that $A \psi=\psi$.

Fix $0<\lambda<1$. Choose $\epsilon>0$ such that $\epsilon+\frac{\lambda^{2}}{4} \leq \frac{\lambda}{2}$. Consider the metric space
\[
X:=\left\{\psi \in \mathcal{C}^{1}([-\epsilon, \epsilon]):|y+\psi(y)| \leq \frac{\lambda}{2} \text { for all } y \in[-\epsilon, \epsilon]\right\}
\]
with the induced supremum metric from $\mathcal{C}^{1}([-\epsilon, \epsilon])$, which we denote by $d$. (Recall: $\mathcal{C}^{1}([-\epsilon, \epsilon])$ is the set of real-valued differentiable functions on $[-\epsilon, \epsilon]$ whose derivative is continuous.)

  1. Show that there is a function $A: X \longrightarrow X$ given by
    \[
    (A \psi)(y)=-(y+\psi(y))^{2}
    \]
  2. Show that if $\psi \in X$ is such that $A \psi=\psi$, then the function $x=y+\psi(y)$ is an inverse to the function $y=x+x^{2}$, locally near the origin.
    In the next few steps, we show that such a $\psi$ exists.
  3. Show that $d\left(A \psi_{1}, A \psi_{2}\right) \leq \lambda d\left(\psi_{1}, \psi_{2}\right)$.
  4. Let $\phi \in X$. Show that the sequence $A^{n} \phi, n \geq 1$ is a Cauchy sequence, and it has a limit. By $A^{n}$, we mean the $n$-fold composition $A \circ A \circ \cdots \circ A$. (You may use the fact that $X$ is complete with respect to d.)
  5. Show that there exists $\psi \in X$ such that $A \psi=\psi$.

questions.questionText: Let $X, Y, Z$ be finite sets. Which of the following statement(s) is/are true? Let $f: X \rightarrow Y, g: Y \rightarrow Z$ be functions. such that the composite function $g \circ f: X \rightarrow Z$ is onto. Then both $g, f$ have to be onto. Assume the number of elements of $X$, denoted as $|X|$, is strictly less than $|Y|$ and also assume that $|X| \leq|Z|$. There exists a one-one function $f: X \rightarrow Y$ and a $g: Y \rightarrow Z$ which is not one-one such that $g \circ f: X \rightarrow Z$ is one-one. Let $i d_{X}$ be the identity function on $X$, i.e. $i d_{X}(x)=x$ for all $x \in X$. Let $f: X \rightarrow Y$ be a function. Then there exists a function $g: Y \rightarrow X$ such that $g \circ f=i d_{X}$ exists. Denote by $i d_{Y}$ the identity function on $Y, i d_{Y}(y)=y$ for all $y \in Y$. Then there exists $g: Y \rightarrow X$ such that $f \circ g=i d_{Y}$ if and only if $f$ is onto.
questions.questionHtml:
Let $X, Y, Z$ be finite sets. Which of the following statement(s) is/are true?

  1. Let $f: X \rightarrow Y, g: Y \rightarrow Z$ be functions. such that the composite function $g \circ f: X \rightarrow Z$ is onto. Then both $g, f$ have to be onto.
  2. Assume the number of elements of $X$, denoted as $|X|$, is strictly less than $|Y|$ and also assume that $|X| \leq|Z|$. There exists a one-one function $f: X \rightarrow Y$ and a $g: Y \rightarrow Z$ which is not one-one such that $g \circ f: X \rightarrow Z$ is one-one.
  3. Let $i d_{X}$ be the identity function on $X$, i.e. $i d_{X}(x)=x$ for all $x \in X$. Let $f: X \rightarrow Y$ be a function. Then there exists a function $g: Y \rightarrow X$ such that $g \circ f=i d_{X}$ exists.
  4. Denote by $i d_{Y}$ the identity function on $Y, i d_{Y}(y)=y$ for all $y \in Y$. Then there exists $g: Y \rightarrow X$ such that $f \circ g=i d_{Y}$ if and only if $f$ is onto.

options.label: A

Let $M_{1}=\left(Q_{1},\left\{q_{1}\right\}, \Delta_{1}, F_{1}\right)$, where $\Delta_{1} \subseteq Q_{1} \times(\Sigma \cup\{\epsilon\}) \times Q_{1}$, be a non deterministic finite automaton (NFA) accepting a language $L_{1} \subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}$. Let $\epsilon$ denote the null string. We construct a new NFA $M_{2}=\left(Q,\left\{q_{2}\right\}, \Delta_{2}, F_{2}\right)$, where $\Delta_{2} \subseteq Q_{2} \times(\Sigma \cup\{\epsilon\}) \times Q_{2}$, as follows.

  • $Q_{2}=Q_{1}$.
  • $q_{2}=q_{1}$.

  • $\left(p, a, p^{\prime}\right) \in \Delta_{2}$ iff either $\left(p, a, p^{\prime}\right) \in \Delta_{1}$ or $\left(p \in F_{1}\right.$ and $a=\epsilon$ and $\left.p^{\prime}=q_{1}\right)$


Prove or disprove: The language $L_{2}$ accepted by $M_{2}$ is $L_{1}^{*}$.

questions.questionText: Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet. The reverse of a word is defined inductively as follows: $\operatorname{rev}(\epsilon)=\epsilon$ and $\operatorname{rev}(w a)=a \cdot \operatorname{rev}(w)$ for $w \in \Sigma^{*}$ and $a \in \Sigma$. For example, $\operatorname{rev}(a a b)=b a a$. For a language $L$, we $\operatorname{define} \operatorname{rev}(L):=\{\operatorname{rev}(w) \mid w \in L\}$. Is $\operatorname{rev}\left(L_{1} \cap L_{2}\right)$ equal to $\operatorname{rev}\left(L_{1}\right) \cap \operatorname{rev}\left(L_{2}\right)$ ? Prove or disprove the following statement: $w \in L \cap \operatorname{rev}(L)$ iff $w=\operatorname{rev}(w)$. Show that if $L$ is regular, $\operatorname{rev}(L)$ is also regular.

questions.questionHtml:
Is there for all context-free grammars a right linear grammar that produces the same language?

  1. Yes, you can find such a grammar by converting to an automaton, and then converting back to a grammar.
  2. Yes, because all right linear grammars are context-free grammars.
  3. No, because not all context-free languages are regular.
  4. No, because not all regular languages are context-free.

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, you can find such a grammar by converting to an automaton, and then converting back to a grammar.

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, because all right linear grammars are context-free grammars.

options.label: C
options.text: No, because not all context-free languages are regular.

options.label: D
options.text: No, because not all regular languages are context-free.

questions.explanation: Answer (c) is correct. We know that the language $\left\{a^{n} b^{n} \mid n \in \mathbb{N}\right\}$ is not regular. But it can be created with this context free grammar: $$ S \rightarrow a S b \mid \lambda $$ So this is a language for which we know for sure that a context-free grammar exists, but not a right linear one. The first and the second answer make no sense because the answer is 'no'. Also, all regular languages are context-free.

questions.questionText: Most languages are case sensitive, so keywords can be written only one way, and the regular expressions describing their lexemes are very simple. However, some languages, like SQL, are case insensitive, so a keyword can be written either in lowercase or in uppercase, or in any mixture of cases. Thus, the SQL keyword SELECT can also be written select, Select, or sEIECT, for instance. Show how to write a regular expression for a keyword in a case-insensitive language. Illustrate the idea by writing the expression for "select" in SQL.

questions.questionText: Let $\Sigma=\{a, b\}$ be an alphabet. A palindrome is a word which reads the same when read from left-to-right, or from right-to-left. For example, the words $a b b a, a b a$ and $a a$ are palindromes, whereas $a a b b$ and $a b$ are not. A palindrome is said to be non-trivial if it has length at least 2 . Let $L$ be the set of all words that contain a non-trivial palindrome as a prefix, that is, $L=\left\{w \in(a+b)^{*} \mid w=u v\right.$ for some non-trivial palindrome $u$ and some $\left.v \in(a+b)^{*}\right\}$ Give an example of a word in $L$, which is not a palindrome. Give three examples of words not in $L$. Suppose $a x \notin L$ for some $x \in \Sigma^{*}$. What can you say about $x$ ? Show that $L$ is regular.

questions.explanation: Question asking about complement of the language accepted by the given automata. As string "abc" is not accepted by the given automata, then string must be member of complement of the language accepted by the automata. A. {Epsilon} doesn't contain "abc" - this is not correct option. B. c*+a*+b* - string "abc" can't generate by this Regular Expression- this is not correct option. C. (a+b)*+(b+c)*+(c+a)*- string "abc" can't generate by this Regular Expression- this is not correct option. Hence, Option D is correct.   What about correct Regular Expression ? Whenever there is 3 different symbols involved in the string, then that string will be rejected by the Automata. So that will be in the complement of the language accepted by the Automata. Note that those three different symbols may be in any order. One possible R.E.= $\epsilon+((a^+.b^+.c^+)+(a^+.c^+.b^+)+(b^+.a^+.c^+)+(b^+.c^+.a^+)+(c^+.b^+.a^+)+(c^+.a^+.b^+)). (a+b+c)^*$ R.E of language accepted by given Automata is $(a+b)^++(

18. Which of the following is true?

  1. There are some regular languages for which no TM exists which accept it
  2. All languages accepted by TM's are infinite
  3. Languages which are not recursive are not accepted by any TM
  4. There are some languages which exist for which no TM exists which accept it

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Languages which are not recursive are not accepted by any TM

options.label: D
options.text: There are some languages which exist for which no TM exists which accept it

questions.explanation: Statement (a): There are some regular languages for which no TM exists which accepts it. This statement is false. Every regular language can be accepted by a finite automaton (FA), and every FA can be simulated by a TM. Therefore, any regular language can also be accepted by a TM. Statement (b): All languages accepted by TM's are infinite. This statement is false. There are many finite languages (languages with a finite number of strings) that can be accepted by TMs. For example, the language {a, b, c} can be accepted by a TM. Statement (c): Languages which are not recursive are not accepted by any TM. This statement is false.If a language is RE(not recursive ) then it will be accepted by turing machine Statement (d): There are some languages which exist for which no TM exists which accepts it. This statement is true. There are languages that are not recursively enumerable, and these languages cannot be accepted by any TM. Such languages are known as non-Turing-recognizable langu

questions.questionText: 1) is $\Sigma = \{a,b, \epsilon\}$ possible? 2) is $L = \{ab,ba, \epsilon\}$ possible? 3) is $\{ \epsilon \}$ a subset of all alphabets or languages? 4) is $\phi = \{ \}$ a subset of all alphabets or languages? where, $\epsilon$ is the empty string.
questions.questionHtml:
1) is $\Sigma = \{a,b, \epsilon\}$ possible?

2) is $L = \{ab,ba, \epsilon\}$ possible?

3) is $\{ \epsilon \}$ a subset of all alphabets or languages?

4) is $\phi = \{ \}$ a subset of all alphabets or languages?

where, $\epsilon$ is the empty string.
questions.explanation: 1) is $\Sigma = \{a,b, \epsilon\}$ possible? - Not possible. Epsilon ($\epsilon$) is a special string whose length is 0. That mean number of input symbols involved in the epsilon is 0. Hence, epsilon is not part of input alphabet. 2) is $L = \{ab,ba, \epsilon\}$ possible? - Yes, possible. Here, epsilon is a string in the language. 3) is $\{ \epsilon \}$ a subset of all alphabets or languages? - Not subset to all languages. It depends upon the language. $\Sigma = \{a,b\}$ and $\Sigma^1 \text{(it is a language)}= \{a,b\}$ - b is a input symbol in $\Sigma$ where as b is a string in $\Sigma^1$. As $\{ \epsilon \}$ is a set which is not $\phi$. Therefore $\{ \epsilon \}$ is not a subset to all languages. 4) is $\phi = \{ \}$ a subset of all languages? - Yes, similar to the Set theory. $\phi$ is trivial set which is subset to all languages. questions.explanation: Regular language and CFL are closed under union operation. So C, D is true. Now, the intersection operation of CFL with regular language is closed, that is CFL itself. A is true. Option $(B)$ is false here.   1. $\mathrm{m}^{2}$
  2. $\mathrm{m}$
  3. $\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{m}+1) / 2$

questions.explanation: Correct Answer is C. The number of substrings that can be formed from a character string of length m is given by the formula: m(m+1)/2 This formula represents the sum of the first m natural numbers and accounts for substrings of all possible lengths, from length 1 to length m.

questions.questionText: There exists a language L d = {M | M doesn't belong to L(M)}. L d is the collection of Turing machines (programs) M such that M does not halt and accept when given itself as input. It is known and proved that L d  is a non-Recursively Enumerable Language. Now L d  can be reduced to the problem A TM  (Universal Language) as follows "To see if w ∈ L d check if <w, w> ∈ A TM ." The theorem 9.7 (Page 393) in Hopcroft Ullman states that if there exists a reduction from P1 to P2, then: if P1 is non RE then so is P2. According to this theorem, since L d  can be reduced to A TM , and L d  is non-RE, A TM  must be non-RE. But we know that A TM   is Recursively Enumerable and undecidable. How is this possible?
questions.questionHtml:
There exists a language Ld = {M | M doesn't belong to L(M)}. Ld is the collection of Turing machines (programs) M such that M does not halt and accept when given itself as input. It is known and proved that Ld is a non-Recursively Enumerable Language.

Now Ld can be reduced to the problem ATM (Universal Language) as follows "To see if w ∈ Ld check if <w, w> ∈ ATM."

The theorem 9.7 (Page 393) in Hopcroft Ullman states that if there exists a reduction from P1 to P2, then: if P1 is non RE then so is P2.

According to this theorem, since Ld can be reduced to ATM, and Ld is non-RE, ATM must be non-RE. But we know that ATM  is Recursively Enumerable and undecidable. How is this possible?

questions.questionText: Which of the following sets has the greatest cardinality? The set of real numbers R The set of all functions from R to {0,1} The set of all finite subsets of natural numbers The set of all finite-length binary strings
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following sets has the greatest cardinality?
  1. The set of real numbers R
  2. The set of all functions from R to {0,1}
  3. The set of all finite subsets of natural numbers
  4. The set of all finite-length binary strings

options.label: A
options.text: The set of real numbers R

options.label: B
options.text: The set of all functions from R to {0,1}

options.label: C
options.text: The set of all finite subsets of natural numbers

options.label: D
options.text: The set of all finite-length binary strings

questions.explanation: Let's compare the cardinalities of the given sets: 1. The set of real numbers R has the cardinality of the continuum, which is uncountably infinite and has the same cardinality as the points on a line. 2. The set of all functions from R to {0,1} has a cardinality strictly greater than the cardinality of the continuum. This is because there are 2^c (where c is the cardinality of R) different functions from R to {0,1}. In other words, it has a larger cardinality than the set of real numbers. 3. The set of all finite subsets of natural numbers has a countably infinite cardinality, which is the same as the cardinality of the natural numbers themselves. 4. The set of all finite-length binary strings also has a countably infinite cardinality. This is because for each positive integer n, there are 2^n different binary strings of length n. Comparing these, the set of all functions from R to {0,1} has the greatest cardinality among the given sets. Bharadwaja1557 answered Feb 7, 2024 Bhara

questions.questionText: Let $n$ be a positive integer, and let \[ S=\{g \in \mathbb{R}[x] \mid g \text { is a polynomial of degree at most } n\}. \] For $g \in S$, let $A_{g}=\left\{x \in \mathbb{R} \mid e^{x}=g(x)\right\} \subset \mathbb{R}$. Let \[ m=\min \left\{\# A_{g} \mid g \in S\right\}, \quad \text { and } \quad M=\max \left\{\# A_{g} \mid g \in S\right\} . \] Then $m=0, M=n$ $m=0, M=n+1$ $m=1, M=n$ $m=1, M=n+1$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $n$ be a positive integer, and let
\[
S=\{g \in \mathbb{R}[x] \mid g \text { is a polynomial of degree at most } n\}.
\]

For $g \in S$, let $A_{g}=\left\{x \in \mathbb{R} \mid e^{x}=g(x)\right\} \subset \mathbb{R}$. Let
\[
m=\min \left\{\# A_{g} \mid g \in S\right\}, \quad \text { and } \quad M=\max \left\{\# A_{g} \mid g \in S\right\} .
\]

Then

  1. $m=0, M=n$
  2. $m=0, M=n+1$
  3. $m=1, M=n$
  4. $m=1, M=n+1$

questions.excerpt: Let $\mathbb{C}$ denote the set of complex numbers and let $k$ be a positive integer. Given a non-zero univariate polynomial $f(x)$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{C}$ and ...
questions.questionText: Let $\mathbb{C}$ denote the set of complex numbers and let $k$ be a positive integer. Given a non-zero univariate polynomial $f(x)$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{C}$ and an $a \in \mathbb{C}$, we say that $a$ is a zero of $f$ of multiplicity $k$ if $f(a)=0, \frac{d^{k} f}{d x^{k}}(a) \neq 0$, and for all $i \in\{1, \ldots, k-1\}$, $\frac{d^{i} f}{d x^{i}}(a)=0$. Which of the following is true for every polynomial $f$ of degree $d$ and every positive integer $k$? The number of distinct zeroes in $\mathbb{C}$ of $f$ of multiplicity $k$ is at most $d / k$, and can be smaller than $d / k$ as well. The number of distinct zeroes in $\mathbb{C}$ of $f$ of multiplicity $k$ is at least $d / k$, and can be larger than $d / k$ as well. The number of distinct zeroes in $\mathbb{C}$ of $f$ of multiplicity $k$ is equal to $d / k$. The number of distinct zeroes in $\mathbb{C}$ of $f$ of multiplicity $k$ is at least $d$, and can be larger than $d$ as well. The number of distinct zeroes in $\mathbb{C}$ of $f$ of multiplicity $k$ is equal to $d$.
questions.questionHtml:

Given a non-zero univariate polynomial $f(x)$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{C}$ and an $a \in \mathbb{C}$, we say that $a$ is a zero of $f$ of multiplicity $k$ if $f(a)=0, \frac{d^{k} f}{d x^{k}}(a) \neq 0$, and for all $i \in\{1, \ldots, k-1\}$, $\frac{d^{i} f}{d x^{i}}(a)=0$.

Which of the following is true for every polynomial $f$ of degree $d$ and every positive integer $k$?

  1. The number of distinct zeroes in $\mathbb{C}$ of $f$ of multiplicity $k$ is at most $d / k$, and can be smaller than $d / k$ as well.
  2. The number of distinct zeroes in $\mathbb{C}$ of $f$ of multiplicity $k$ is at least $d / k$, and can be larger than $d / k$ as well.
  3. The number of distinct zeroes in $\mathbb{C}$ of $f$ of multiplicity $k$ is equal to $d / k$.
  4. The number of distinct zeroes in $\mathbb{C}$ of $f$ of multiplicity $k$ is at least $d$, and can be larger than $d$ as well.
  5. The number of distinct zeroes in $\mathbb{C}$ of $f$ of multiplicity $k$ is equal to $d$.

questions.questionText: In the $n$-queens completion problem, the input is an $n \times n$ chess board with queens on some squares, and the goal is to determine if there is a way to place more queens so that the total number of queens is $n$ and no two queens attack each other (two queens are said to attack each other if they are on the same row, or they are on the same column, or they are on the same diagonal). Consider the following statements: The $n$-queens completion problem is decidable. The $n$-queens completion problem is decidable in time $O\left(n^{n^{n}}\right)$. The problem of "checking whether a given program solves the $n$-queens completion problem" is decidable. The problem of "checking whether a given program solves the $n$-queens completion problem in time $O\left(n^{n^{n}}\right)$ " is decidable. The problem of "checking whether a given program solves the $n$-queens completion problem" is decidable in time $O\left(n^{n^{n}}\right)$. Which of the above is true? Only $\text{(i) and (ii)}$. Only $\text{(i) and (iii)}$. Only $\text{(i), (ii) and (iv)}$. Only $\text{(iii),(iv) and (v)}$. Only $\text{(i), (iii) and (iv)}$.
questions.questionHtml:
In the $n$-queens completion problem, the input is an $n \times n$ chess board with queens on some squares, and the goal is to determine if there is a way to place more queens so that the total number of queens is $n$ and no two queens attack each other (two queens are said to attack each other if they are on the same row, or they are on the same column, or they are on the same diagonal).

Consider the following statements:

  1. The $n$-queens completion problem is decidable.
  2. The $n$-queens completion problem is decidable in time $O\left(n^{n^{n}}\right)$.
  3. The problem of "checking whether a given program solves the $n$-queens completion problem" is decidable.
  4. The problem of "checking whether a given program solves the $n$-queens completion problem in time $O\left(n^{n^{n}}\right)$ " is decidable.
  5. The problem of "checking whether a given program solves the $n$-queens completion problem" is decidable in time $O\left(n^{n^{n}}\right)$.

Which of the above is true?

  1. Only $\text{(i) and (ii)}$.
  2. Only $\text{(i) and (iii)}$.
  3. Only $\text{(i), (ii) and (iv)}$.
  4. Only $\text{(iii),(iv) and (v)}$.
  5. Only $\text{(i), (iii) and (iv)}$.

questions.excerpt: A subset $\text{S}$ of the rational numbers is said to be "nice" if for every infinite sequence of $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ of elements from $\text{S}$, there is always two ind...
questions.questionText: A subset $\text{S}$ of the rational numbers is said to be "nice" if for every infinite sequence of $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ of elements from $\text{S}$, there is always two indices $i<j$ such that $x_i \leq x_j$. Consider the following statements. The set of natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ is "nice". The set of integers $\mathbb{Z}$ is "nice". The set of positive rational numbers is "nice". Which of the above statements is/are true? Only $\text{(i)}$. Only $\text{(i)}$ and $\text{(ii)}$. Only $\text{(i)}$ and $\text{(iii)}$. All three statements are true. None of the three statements is true.
questions.questionHtml:
A subset $\text{S}$ of the rational numbers is said to be "nice" if for every infinite sequence of $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ of elements from $\text{S}$, there is always two indices $i<j$ such that $x_i \leq x_j$. Consider the following statements.

  1. The set of natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ is "nice".
  2. The set of integers $\mathbb{Z}$ is "nice".
  3. The set of positive rational numbers is "nice".

Which of the above statements is/are true?

  1. Only $\text{(i)}$.
  2. Only $\text{(i)}$ and $\text{(ii)}$.
  3. Only $\text{(i)}$ and $\text{(iii)}$.
  4. All three statements are true.
  5. None of the three statements is true.
questions.explanation: 1. The Natural Numbers (N) The natural numbers are well-ordered. Any infinite sequence of natural numbers will eventually contain a non-decreasing pair because there are no infinite strictly decreasing sequences in (N). For example: Consider any sequence, e.g., 5,3,1,2,4,…. After a finite number of decreases, the sequence must stabilize and start increasing or repeating (since N is finite below any value). Thus, N satisfies the "nice" property. Conclusion: N is "nice." 2. The Integers (Z) Now consider the integers. It is possible to construct an infinite strictly decreasing sequence in Z. For example: xn=−n(e.g., −1,−2,−3,…) Here, for every i<j, xi>xj​, so there is no non-decreasing pair. This violates the "nice" property. Conclusion: Z is not "nice." 3. questions.explanation: The question is asking if given language is CFL or not. In the answer it tells it is, and how. L = $0^{m}$$1^{n}$$1^{m}$$0^{n}$ Assuming you are not friendly with the working of how CFLs are accepted: We know CFL uses a stack(PDA) to keep track of the language: Say you want to know if $a^{k}$$b^{k}$ is CFL or not; You make a stack, have an initial symbol in stack (at top, say Z), push another symbol K for every a inputted (k times).Then on encountering b everytime, you pop a K from the top of the stack. For this language, if no of times b inputted = no of times of a, then language is accepted, so at the end all Ks put in stack by a are popped by b, we get Z back on top again and its accepted (PDA by final state) In this case , as we cannot directly compare $0^{m}$ with $1^{n}$ on the stack, we re-arrange the terms as    $0^{m}$$1^{m}$$1^{n}$$0^{n}$. questions.questionText: Imagine a Turing machine that needs to determine whether a computation will halt or continue when provided with a specific input. However, there's a twist: the Turing machine has the ability to send messages backward in time. Problem Description: Setup: The Turing machine is given an input tape with symbols.. It has the ability to send a single bit message back in time before the computation starts. Time-Traveling Rules: The Turing machine can send a single bit (0 or 1) back in time to its past self. The message is sent only once before the computation begins. The message can influence the decision-making process during the computation. Objective: Determine whether the computation will halt or continue.. The Turing machine must make its decision based on the original input and the information received from its future self. Challenges: The Turing machine needs to handle self-consistency paradoxes. questions.questionHtml:
Imagine a Turing machine that needs to determine whether a computation will halt or continue when provided with a specific input. However, there's a twist: the Turing machine has the ability to send messages backward in time.

Problem Description:

  1. Setup:

    The Turing machine is given an input tape with symbols.. It has the ability to send a single bit message back in time before the computation starts.

  2. Time-Traveling Rules:

    The Turing machine can send a single bit (0 or 1) back in time to its past self. The message is sent only once before the computation begins. The message can influence the decision-making process during the computation.

  3. Objective:

    Determine whether the computation will halt or continue.. The Turing machine must make its decision based on the original input and the information received from its future self.

  4. Challenges:

    The Turing machine needs to handle self-consistency paradoxes. For example, if it decides to halt based on a future message, the future message might not be sent if it decides to continue. The time-traveling aspect introduces non-determinism and complexity in decision-making.

  5. Scoring:

    The challenge is considered successfully solved if the Turing machine correctly decides whether to halt or continue, considering the time-traveling information.

Source: This Questions is generated by ChatGPT, still it is interesting whether it is possible to design the turing machine or not?

questions.title: Test Series: Is null string considered as a proper prefix of any string? According to me, total number of proper prefixes for n length string should be (n-1), can anyone please get this point cleared.
questions.excerpt: Question No. 25Awarded Marks: 0In a string of length $n$, which of the following is/are true?Options Correct sequence of options.A: Number of Prefixes are nB : Number of ...
questions.questionText: Question No. 25 Awarded Marks: 0 In a string of length $n$, which of the following is/are true? Options Correct sequence of options. A: Number of Prefixes are n B : Number of Proper prefixes are $\mathrm{n}-1$ Your Selection C : Number of Suffixes are $\mathrm{n}+1$ Your Selection Correct Option D: Number of Subsequences are $2^{n}$ Your Selection Correct Option Explaination Answer: (c) and (d) A) $n+1$ ( $n$ prefixes for $n$ characters, plus the empty string) B) $n(n+1$ prefixes for $n$ characters, minus the string itself $)$ C) $\mathrm{n}+1$ (similar to (a))
questions.questionHtml:
Question No. 25
Awarded Marks: 0

In a string of length $n$, which of the following is/are true?

Options Correct sequence of options.
A: Number of Prefixes are n

B : Number of Proper prefixes are $\mathrm{n}-1$ Your Selection
C : Number of Suffixes are $\mathrm{n}+1$
Your Selection
Correct Option

D: Number of Subsequences are
$2^{n}$
Your Selection
Correct Option

Explaination
Answer: (c) and (d)
A) $n+1$ ( $n$ prefixes for $n$ characters, plus the empty string)
B) $n(n+1$ prefixes for $n$ characters, minus the string itself $)$
C) $\mathrm{n}+1$ (similar to (a))
questions.explanation: Just relate it with proper subset concept of set theory suppose, set A ={1,2,3,4} Its proper subset is any subset of A that contains atleast 1 element less than A, that means A is not a proper subset of itself. but as empty set (phi) $\Phi$ is a subset of A that has atleast 1 element less than A so it is also a proper subset of A. infact in general the empty set (phi) is a proper subset of every set except for the empty set, and no set is a proper subset of itself.   Similarly, if String S= “abcd” then, empty string epsilon($\epsilon$) is also one of its prefixes. So its prefixes are $\epsilon$, a , ab, abc , abcd but since option b talks about proper prefix, then abcd is not considered, because “A proper prefix of a string is a prefix that is not equal to the string itself”. hence proper prefixes are  $\epsilon$ , a , ab , abc Thus for a ‘n’ length string, the number of proper prefixes = n. prajjwal_191 answered Nov 26, 2023 • edited Nov 26, 2023 by prajjwal_191 prajjw

questions.questionText: Which of the following statement is not correct? If $L$ is accepted by NFA, then there exists a DFA that accepts $L$ If $L$ is accepted by an NFA with $\in$ transition, then $L$ can be accepted by NFA without $\epsilon$ transition If $L$ is accepted by a non-deterministic PDA then it is not always true that $L$ is also accepted by deterministic PDA If $L$ is accepted by turing Machine, which halts on every w in $L$ then $L^{\prime}$ is recursively enumerable but not recursive
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following statement is not correct?

  1. If $L$ is accepted by NFA, then there exists a DFA that accepts $L$
  2. If $L$ is accepted by an NFA with $\in$ transition, then $L$ can be accepted by NFA without $\epsilon$ transition
  3. If $L$ is accepted by a non-deterministic PDA then it is not always true that $L$ is also accepted by deterministic PDA
  4. If $L$ is accepted by turing Machine, which halts on every w in $L$ then $L^{\prime}$ is recursively enumerable but not recursive

options.label: D

https://gateoverflow.in/?qa=blob&qa_blobid=15872129177586526309
questions.explanation: L is definitely a regular language. You are incorrectly using the Pumping Lemma. The pumping lemma states that if L is regular, than (as in your case) there exists a combination of x, y, z such that (...conditions...).  Here the word ' there exists ' is important, it is not ' for every '.  Here pumping lemma works when we take for eg x = a y = aaa z = empty string

questions.questionHtml:
Here's the operator precedence for regular expressions, from highest to lowest:
$$
\begin{gathered}
(\text{R}) \\
\text{R}^* \\
\text{R}_1 \text{R}_2 \\
\text{R}_1 \cup \text{R}_2
\end{gathered}
$$

Consider the regular expression
$$ab^*c\cup d$$

How many of the strings below are in the language described by this regular expression?

  • $ababc$
  • $abd$
  • $ac$
  • $abcd$

questions.explanation: $\color{red}{\text{Detailed Video Solution:}}$   https://youtu.be/XF2ygVBjlTg?t=125 The language $\emptyset$ is empty, which means that it contains no words. All other languages are equal to $\{\lambda\}$. If you concatenate zero words from the empty language, you get the empty word. If you concatenate zero or more times the empty word, it will still be the empty word. Correct Answer: A

questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following four languages is different from the other three?

  1. $(\{a, b\})^*$
  2. $(\{b, a, a\})^*$
  3. $\left(\{a\}^* \cup\{b\}^*\right)$
  4. $(\{a\} \cup\{b\})^*$
questions.explanation: $\color{red}{\text{Detailed Video Solution:}}$   https://youtu.be/XF2ygVBjlTg?t=596   The languages $(\{a, b\})^*,(\{b, a, a\})^*$, and $(\{a\} \cup\{b\})^*$ basically all state: choose either $a$ or $b$ and do that as often as you want. This gives all words over the alphabet $\{a, b\}$. The language $\left(\{a\}^* \cup\{b\}^*\right)$, however, states: take any amount of $a$'s or any amount of $b$'s. In particular this last language doesn't contain words like $a b$ that contain $a$'s and $b$'s. Regular expression for $(\{a, b\})^*,(\{b, a, a\})^*$, and $(\{a\} \cup\{b\})^*$ is $(a+b)^*$ Regular expression for $\left(\{a\}^* \cup\{b\}^*\right)$ is $a^* + b^*$ Correct Answer: C

questions.questionText: Is the complement of a regular language always regular? Yes, because the regular languages are exactly the languages that can be recognized with a DFA, and it is easy to construct a DFA for the complement. Yes, because the complement of the complement is the language itself, so no information is lost by complementation. No, because the complement symbol $\overline{\text{L}}$ is not allowed in a regular expression. No, because if the words in a language are regular, all words that are not regular will be in the complement.

  3. No, because the complement symbol $\overline{\text{L}}$ is not allowed in a regular expression.

questions.explanation: $\color{red}{\text{Detailed Video Solution:}}$   https://youtu.be/XF2ygVBjlTg?t=1746 It is true that the regular languages correspond to the languages generated by DFAs. By swapping all final states and non-final states in a DFA, we can compute the complement of a language with a new DFA, which by definition corresponds to a regular language again. The option $B$ is saying that "Yes, because $\bar {\bar L} = L$". This is true for all langauge but this is not correct reason/answer to the given question. The third and the fourth option make no sense because the answer is 'yes'. Correct Answer: A

Yes, when there is a word $w$ for which any extension $w w^{\prime}$ will not be in the language. Yes, because each state needs to have a transition for each symbol.   1. Yes, when there is a word $w$ for which any extension $w w^{\prime}$ will not be in the language.
  2. Yes, because each state needs to have a transition for each symbol.
  3. No, because you can always split a sink in multiple states.
  4. No, because you can always use a non-deterministic automaton.

questions.explanation: $\color{red}{\text{Detailed Video Solution:}}$  Detailed Video Solution (Must Watch)   The idea of a sink is that you create a 'black hole' in a DFA: once you get in there, you can never get out anymore. This can be done using a single state with the 'sink property'. However, it can also be done using two non-final states $q$ and $q^{\prime},$ where for each symbol $s$ in the alphabet we have $\delta(q, s)=q^{\prime}$ and $\delta\left(q^{\prime}, s\right)=q$. This has the same effect, but the 'looping' is not done directly to a single state, but indirectly between two states. The first and the second answer make no sense because the answer is 'no'. The fourth answer makes no sense because the question was about deterministic automata, and what is possible in a non-deterministic automaton is irrelevant for this. Correct Answer: C Helpful Comment:   https://gateoverflow.in/408475/classes-weekly-finite-automata-regular-expression-question?show=408774#c408774

\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, y\right)
$$

questions.explanation: Detailed Video Solution, with Complete Analysis:  https://youtu.be/ldychl4M6fE?t=2359 Since $\delta^*()$ is a function, the following hold $$ \begin{aligned} \text { Reflexive } & \delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right) \\ \text { Symmetric } & \left(\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, y\right)\right) \Rightarrow\left(\delta^*\left(q_0, y\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)\right) \\ \text { Transitive } & \left(\left(\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, y\right)\right) \wedge\left(\delta^*\left(q_0, y\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, z\right)\right)\right) \Rightarrow\left(\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, z\right)\right) \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, indistinguishable is an equivalence relation on strings. NOTE:  If strings $x, y$ are indistinguishable then $xw, yw$ are also indistinguishable, for all strings $w$. Easy to prove, by definition $\&$ properties of a DFA. questions.questionText: If for a language $\text{L}$ is given that $\text{L}^*=\text{L},$ what does not necessarily follow? $\text{L L = L}$ $\lambda \in \text{L}$ $\text{L}$ is infinite $\text{L}$ is non-empty
questions.questionHtml:
If for a language $\text{L}$ is given that $\text{L}^*=\text{L},$ what does not necessarily follow?

  1. $\text{L L = L}$
  2. $\lambda \in \text{L}$
  3. $\text{L}$ is infinite
  4. $\text{L}$ is non-empty
questions.explanation: Detailed Video Solution, with Complete Analysis:  https://youtu.be/ldychl4M6fE?t=4605 If $\text{L}=\{\lambda\}$, then $\text{L}^*=\text{L}$. So the assumption that $\text{L}^*=\text{L}$ does not imply that $\text{L}$ is infinite. Statement $\text{LL}=\text{L}$ holds, because if $w \in \text{LL},$ then $w=w_1 w_2 \in L^*=\text{L}$, and if $w \in \text{L},$ then $w=w \lambda \in \text{LL},$ because by definition $\lambda \in \text{L}^*$ and hence $\lambda \in \text{L}$. Statement $\lambda \in \text{L}$ holds, because by definition $\lambda \in \text{L}^*,$ and hence $\lambda \in \text{L}$. Statement $\text{L}$ is non-empty holds, because if $\text{L}=\emptyset$, then $\text{L}^*=\{\lambda\}$ which contradicts $\text{L}^*=\text{L}$. Correct Answer: C

questions.explanation: Statement 'if $w \in \text{L}^*$ then also $w^\text{R} \in \text{L}^*$' holds. Let $w \in \text{L}^*$. Then there exists $k \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $w=w_1 \cdots w_k$ and $w_i \in \text{L}$ for $i \in\{1, \ldots, k\}$. Note that $w^\text{R}=\left(w_1 \cdots w_k\right)^\text{R}=w_k^\text{R} \cdots w_1^\text{R}$. However, because $\text{L}^\text{R}=\text{L}$, we have that $w_i^\text{R} \in \text{L}$ for $i \in\{1, \ldots, k\}$. Hence $w^\text{R}=w_k^\text{R} \cdots w_1^\text{R} \in \text{L}^*$. Statement 'there is a $w \in \text{L}$ for which also $w^\text{R} \in \text{L}$ ' does not hold. Take $\text{L}=\emptyset$. Then $\text{L}^\text{R}=\emptyset=\text{L}$. However, there is no $w \in \text{L}$, so certainly no $w \in \text{L}$ for which $w^\text{R} \in \text{L}$. Statement ' $\lambda \in \text{L}$, because $\lambda^\text{R}=\lambda$ ' does not hold. Let be given a language $\text{L}$. Which of the following languages is not necessarily equal to the others?

  1. $\text{L L}^*$

questions.explanation: Note that if $\lambda \notin \text{L},$ then $\text{L L}^*$ does not include $\lambda$ and therefore $\text{L L}^*$ is not necessarily equal to the other three languages. Also note that $\text{L L}^* = \text{L}^+$. $\text{L}^* = \text{L}^0 + \text{L}^ 1+ \text{L}^2 + \text{L}^3 + \dots$ So, $\text{L L}^* = \text{L} (\text{L}^0 + \text{L}^ 1+ \text{L}^2 + \text{L}^3 + \dots) = \text{L}^ 1+ \text{L}^2 + \text{L}^3 + \dots = \text{L}^+$ GO Classes answered Aug 3, 2023 • edited 16 hours ago by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow See all 2 Comments 2 2 Comments reply Roshni Choudhary commented Mar 22, 2025 reply Follow flag but L* already contains lemda ,so how its different from others 1 1 reply Share Abhinav_verma commented Oct 30, 2025 reply Follow flag L* conatins lemda its true but when it multiplies with L (not containg lemda) its result in to L  L.L* = L.  = L(not containg lemda) 1 1 reply Share Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following regular expressions describes a language different from the others?

  1. $(a \cup b)^*$
  2. $\left(a^* b^*\right)^*$
  3. $\left(b^* a^*\right)^*$
  4. $\left(a^* \cup b^*\right)$
questions.explanation: Note that $$ \mathcal{L}\left((a \cup b)^*\right)=\mathcal{L}\left(\left(a^* b^*\right)^*\right)=\mathcal{L}\left(\left(b^* a^*\right)^*\right)=\{a, b\}^* $$ and that $$ \mathcal{L}\left(a^* \cup b^*\right)=\{a\}^* \cup\{b\}^* $$ So in particular $a b \notin\{a\}^* \cup\{b\}^*$, but $a b \in\{a, b\}^*$. Correct Answer: D

questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following regular expressions describes a language different from the others?

  1. $a^* b^*$
  2. $(\lambda \cup a a)^*(\lambda \cup b b)^*$
  3. $(a \cup a a)^*(b \cup b b)^*$
  4. $(\lambda \cup a)^*(\lambda \cup b)^*$
questions.explanation: Note that $$ \mathcal{L}\left(a^* b^*\right)=\mathcal{L}\left((a \cup a a)^*(b \cup b b)^*\right)=\mathcal{L}\left((\lambda \cup a)^*(\lambda \cup b)^*\right)=\left\{a^n b^m \mid n, m \in \mathbb{N}\right\} $$ and that $$ \mathcal{L}\left((\lambda \cup a a)^*(\lambda \cup b b)^*\right)=\left\{a^{2 n} b^{2 m} \mid n, m \in \mathbb{N}\right\} $$ So in particular $a b \notin\left\{a^{2 n} b^{2 m} \mid n, m \in \mathbb{N}\right\}$, but $a b \in\left\{a^n b^m \mid n, m \in \mathbb{N}\right\}$. Correct Answer: B

questions.questionText: Let $\Sigma= {a, b}$ and language $\text{L} = {aa, bb}$. Then, the complement of $\text{L}$ is ________. $\left\{\lambda, a, b, ab, ba \right\} \cup \left\{w \in\left\{a, b\right\}^{*} | |w| > 3 \right\}$ $\left\{a, b, ab, ba \right\} \cup \left\{w  \in \left\{a, b\right\}^{*} | |w| \geq 3 \right\}$  $\left\{w \in  \left\{a, b\right\}^{*} | |w| > 3\right\} \cup \left\{a, b, ab, ba \right\}$  $\left\{\lambda, a, b, ab, ba\right\} \cup \left\{w \in \left\{a, b\right\}^{*} | |w| \geq 3 \right\}$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $\Sigma= {a, b}$ and language $\text{L} = {aa, bb}$. Then, the complement of $\text{L}$ is ________.

  1. $\left\{\lambda, a, b, ab, ba \right\} \cup \left\{w \in\left\{a, b\right\}^{*} | |w| > 3 \right\}$
  2. $\left\{a, b, ab, ba \right\} \cup \left\{w  \in \left\{a, b\right\}^{*} | |w| \geq 3 \right\}$ 
  3. $\left\{w \in  \left\{a, b\right\}^{*} | |w| > 3\right\} \cup \left\{a, b, ab, ba \right\}$ 
  4. $\left\{\lambda, a, b, ab, ba\right\} \cup \left\{w \in \left\{a, b\right\}^{*} | |w| \geq 3 \right\}$
questions.explanation: Alphabet $\sum= a,b$  and language $L=aa,bb$. So, complement of language wil be  $L’ = \{w | w\in \{a,b\}^* where \ w \ \text{will not contain aa, bb}\}$ So, $L’$ will contain $\{\lambda, a,b,ab,ba\}$ as they are not in $L$ and also the set of strings whose length is atleast $3$ which are also not in $L$. Finally, $L’=\{\lambda, a,b,ab,ba\} \cup \{w\in\{a,b\}^*||w|\geq3\}$ $\color{Green}Ans: D$ SilentClimber answered Jul 21, 2023 SilentClimber comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes L = {aa,bb}. So L’ = {w | w belongs to {a,b}* and w not equal to aa,bb}. So, L’ contains all strings of length atleast 3. Also, it contains strings of length 0 and 1 i.e {e,a,b}. It also contains ab and ba as they are not in L. So L’ = {e,a,b,ab,ba} U {w| w belongs to {a,b}* where |w|>=3} aravind1278 answered Jul 20, 2023 aravind1278 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes Checking optionwise: In option A, 3

questions.explanation: To design a Moore machine that recognizes the pattern 01011 and generates an output of 1 when the pattern is found, we can follow these steps: 1. Define the states: We need three states for this machine: S0, S1, and S2. S0 will be the initial state, and S2 will be the accepting state where the output will be 1. 2. Define the inputs: Since the input is a binary stream, we have a single input, which we can label as "I". 3. Define the outputs: We have a single output, which we can label as "O". 4. Define the state transitions and outputs: State | Input | Next State | Output ------|-------|------------|------- S0    | 0     | S0         | 0 S0    | 1     | S1         | 0 S1    | 0     | S2         | 0 S1    | 1    &nbs

questions.explanation: To find the regular expression (R.E.) for a finite automaton (FA) given its transition equations, we can follow these steps: Step 1: Assign a variable to each state of the FA. In this case, we have four states: q1, q2, q3, and q4. Step 2: Write down the equations for each state transition. - q4 = q3 1 - q3 = q2 0 - q2 = q1 1 + q2 1 + q4 1 - q1 = ε + q1 0 + q3 0 + q4 0 Step 3: Eliminate ε-transitions (ε is the empty string) by substitution. - q1 = 0 + q3 0 + q4 0 - q2 = q1 1 + q2 1 + q4 1 - q3 = q2 0 - q4 = q3 1 Step 4: Substitute the variables with regular expressions to eliminate the equations. - q1 = 0 + (q2 0) 0 + (q3 1) 0 - q2 = (q1 1 + q2 1 + q4 1) - q3 = (q2 0) - q4 = (q3 1) Step 5: Solve the resulting system of equations using the method of regular expression algebra. To simplify the expressions, let's assign a new variable for each subexpression: - A = (q2 0) - B = (q3 1) - C = (q1 1 + q2 1 + q4 1) Now we can substitute these variables in the equations: - q1 = 0 + A0 + B0

questions.questionHtml:
Q. l1 = a*+b* and l2 = a*b*. which of the following is true?

a. l1 = l2

b. l1 U l2=(a+b)*

c. l1*=l2*

d. none
questions.explanation: When you expand l1 and l2 you will find, l1 = {€, a, b, aa, bb, aaa, bbb,....} l2 = {€, a,aa, aaa, b ,bb, bbb, ab, aabb,abbb,aaab, .....} So in this you can clearly find that l1 and l2 are containing same elements so option 1 is false. l1 U l2 = {€, a, aa, aaa, b, bb, bbb, ab, aabb, aaaab, abbbb,.......} (a+b)*= {€, a, aa, aaa, b, bb, bbb,  ab, aabb, abbb,aaab,  bba, bbbaaaa, ........} So, l1 U l2 containing all the strings in which 'a' or 'b' are present and 'a' is appearing before 'b'. But this is not true for (a+b)* that's why option 2 is also incorrect. Now kleene star of l1 is nothing but (a+b)* and l2 is also can be written in the form of (a+b)* so the option 3 is correct for this problem.   Hope this explanation is helpful.

questions.questionHtml:
For $S \rightarrow 0S1 | \epsilon$ for $\sum=\{0,1\}^*$, which of the following is wrong for the language produced?

(a) Non regular language

(b) $0^n1^n | n\geq0$

(c) $0^n1^n | n\geq1$

(d) None of the mentioned
questions.explanation: Answer: C Options A and B are correct.   Explanation: A: For the given language that generates epsilon or an equal number of zeros followed by an equal number of ones, we cannot design finite automata as the count of the variables cannot be accounted for. So, PDA would do the job. Therefore, the language is non-regular. B: At n=0 generates epsilon and at n=1,2..so on generates an equal number of zeros followed by an equal number of ones. Therefore satisfy the given language. C: Here the epsilon cannot be generated.

questions.questionText: A $k$-term $T=\ell_{1} \wedge \ell_{2} \wedge \cdots \wedge \ell_{r}$ is defined to be a conjunction of at most $k$ literals, where each literal $\ell_{i}$ is a Boolean variable or its negation and $r \leq k$. A formula $\Phi$ is said to be a $k$-$\text{DNF}$ if it is of the form $T_{1} \vee T_{2} \vee \ldots \cdots \vee T_{m}$ where each $T_{i}$ is a $k$-term. An assignment of $\text{TRUE/FALSE}$ values to the variables appearing in a formula $\Phi$ is said to be a satisfying assignment for $\Phi$ if, under the assignment, $\Phi$ evaluates to $\text{TRUE}$. Otherwise, the assignment is said to be a violating assignment for $\Phi$. Consider the following statements $\text{(S1)}$ Given a $\text{2-DNF}$ $\Phi$, one can find a violating assignment for $\Phi$ in polynomial time. $\text{(S2)}$ It is $\text{NP}$-hard to find a violating assignment for a given $\text{3-DNF}$ $\Phi$. $\text{(S3)}$ Given a $\text{3-DNF}$ $\Phi$, one can find a satisfying assignment for $\Phi$ in polynomial time. Which of the following statements are correct? Statements $\text{(S1), (S2)}$, and $\text{(S3)}$ are all true. Statements $\text{(S1)}$ and $\text{(S2)}$ are true, but statement $\text{(S3)}$ is not known to be true. Statements $\text{(S2)}$ is true, but statements $\text{(S1)}$ and $\text{(S3)}$ are not known to be true. Statements $\text{(S1), (S2)}$, and $\text{(S3)}$ are false. Statements $\text{(S1)}$ and $\text{(S3)}$ are true, but $\text{(S2)}$ is not known to be true.

In $1st$ path, compare first occurrences of $a's$ with $b's$ by first removing last occurrences of $a's$. $ \implies\underbrace{aaaaaa} \$ aaaaa \$ \underbrace{bbbbb} \$ $  4. In $2nd$ path, compare second occurences of $a's$ (i.e. $a's$ after first $\$$) with $b's$ $ \implies {aaaaaa} \$ \underbrace{aaaaa} \$ \underbrace{bbbbb} \$ $  5. Now in both the path, if $\#a's \geqslant \#b's$ then accept it. If one of the path accepts, that means $\#k's \le max(i,j)$  Complement of $L$ is not CFL. questions.explanation: The regular expression is given as $\text{letter(letter+digit)*}$. This regular expression accepts the strings of one occurrence of a letter followed by any occurrence of letter and digits, such as $\text{(letter,letter.letter,letter.digit,letter.digit.digit..$\infty$)}$ Option (A) This is wrong because it also accepts empty string that is  $\epsilon$.   Option (B):  This is wrong because it accepts strings like $\text{(letter), (letter.letter) ...(letter.digit) ,(letter.digit.digit)}$, but it will not accepts the strings like $\text{(letter.digit.letter)}$.  Option (C):  It is the correct option. it will accepts all the strings of $\text{letter(letter+digit)*}$. Option (D): it is wrong. it RE is $\text{(letter(letter. digit)*)}$ and it will accept strings like ${(letter),(letter.letter.digit).(letter.letter.digit.letter.digit)...\infty}$.  it will not accepts strings like $(letter. letter),(letter. digit)$ etc.

questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following statements is/are $\text{CORRECT}?$

  1. The intersection of two regular languages is regular.
  2. The intersection of two context-free languages is context-free.
  3. The intersection of two recursive languages is recursive.
  4. The intersection of two recursively enumerable languages is recursively enumerable.

options.label: A
options.text: The intersection of two regular languages is regular.

options.label: B
options.text: The intersection of two context-free languages is context-free.

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.explanation: (A)  The intersection of two recursively enumerable languages is recursively enumerable. This statement is true because REL is closed under intersection operations. This is true because REC language is closed under intersection operations. (D) The intersection of two regular languages is regular. questions.questionText: Consider the context-free grammar $G$ below \[ \begin{array}{l} S \rightarrow a S b \mid X \\ X \rightarrow a X \mid X b \mid a \mid b, \end{array} \] where $S$ and $X$ are non-terminals, and $a$ and $b$ are terminal symbols. The starting non-terminal is $S$. Which one of the following statements is $\text{CORRECT}?$ The language generated by $G$ is $(a+b)^{\ast}$ The language generated by $G$ is $a^{\ast}(a+b) b^{\ast}$ The language generated by $G$ is $a^{\ast} b^{\ast}(a+b)$ The language generated by $G$ is not a regular language
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the context-free grammar $G$ below
\[
\begin{array}{l}
S \rightarrow a S b \mid X \\
X \rightarrow a X \mid X b \mid a \mid b,
\end{array}
\]
where $S$ and $X$ are non-terminals, and $a$ and $b$ are terminal symbols. The starting non-terminal is $S$.

Which one of the following statements is $\text{CORRECT}?$

  1. The language generated by $G$ is $(a+b)^{\ast}$
  2. The language generated by $G$ is $a^{\ast}(a+b) b^{\ast}$
  3. The language generated by $G$ is $a^{\ast} b^{\ast}(a+b)$
  4. The language generated by $G$ is not a regular language

options.label: B
options.text: The language generated by $G$ is $a^{\ast}(a+b) b^{\ast}$

options.label: C
options.text: The language generated by $G$ is $a^{\ast} b^{\ast}(a+b)$

options.label: D
options.text: The language generated by $G$ is not a regular language

questions.explanation: Given productions of grammar G : S → aSb / X   X → aX / Xb / a / b    NOTE : While finding the expression for any given Grammar G, always try to solve in bottom up fashion.    For X : In X, any number of a & b can occur and when we wish to terminate, we have choice between a & b.   So, X → $a^{m}(a+b) / (a+b)b^{p}$ $(m \geq 0, p \geq 0)$   Replace this X in above productions. Then productions will look like this : S → aSb / $a^{m}(a+b) / (a+b)b^{p}$.   For S : Let’s first analyze S → aSb S → aSb S → aaSbb S → aaaSbbb    This is simply, $a^{n}b^{n}$ ($n\geq 1$). Let’s Substitute this :   S → $a^{n}a^{m}(a+b)b^{n} / a^{n}(a+b)b^{p}b^{n}$   This can further be simplified as :  $a^{*}(a+b)b^{*}$ Option B , is correct answer.

questions.questionText: Consider the pushdown automaton $\text{(PDA)}\;P$ below, which runs on the input alphabet $\{a, b\}$, has stack alphabet $\{\perp, A\}$, and has three states $\{s, p, q\}$, with $s$ being the start state. A transition from state $u$ to state $v$, labelled $c / X / \gamma$, where $c$ is an input symbol or $\epsilon, X$ is a stack symbol, and $\gamma$ is a string of stack symbols, represents the fact that in state $u$, the $\text{(PDA)}$ can read $c$ from the input, with $X$ on the top of its stack, pop $X$ from the stack, push in the string $\gamma$ on the stack, and go to state $v$. In the initial configuration, the stack has only the symbol $\perp$ in it. The $\text{(PDA)}$ accepts by empty stack. Which one of the following options correctly describes the language accepted by $P ?$ $\left\{a^{m} b^{n} \mid 1 \leq m\right.$ and $\left.n \lt m\right\}$ $\left\{a^{m} b^{n} \mid 0 \leq n \leq m\right\}$ $\left\{a^{m} b^{n} \mid 0 \leq m\right.$ and $\left.0 \leq n\right\}$ $\left\{a^{m} \mid 0 \leq m\right\} \cup\left\{b^{n} \mid 0 \leq n\right\}$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the pushdown automaton $\text{(PDA)}\;P$ below, which runs on the input alphabet $\{a, b\}$, has stack alphabet $\{\perp, A\}$, and has three states $\{s, p, q\}$, with $s$ being the start state. A transition from state $u$ to state $v$, labelled $c / X / \gamma$, where $c$ is an input symbol or $\epsilon, X$ is a stack symbol, and $\gamma$ is a string of stack symbols, represents the fact that in state $u$, the $\text{(PDA)}$ can read $c$ from the input, with $X$ on the top of its stack, pop $X$ from the stack, push in the string $\gamma$ on the stack, and go to state $v$. In the initial configuration, the stack has only the symbol $\perp$ in it. The $\text{(PDA)}$ accepts by empty stack.

Which one of the following options correctly describes the language accepted by $P ?$

  1. $\left\{a^{m} b^{n} \mid 1 \leq m\right.$ and $\left.n \lt m\right\}$
  2. $\left\{a^{m} b^{n} \mid 0 \leq n \leq m\right\}$
  3. $\left\{a^{m} b^{n} \mid 0 \leq m\right.$ and $\left.0 \leq n\right\}$
  4. $\left\{a^{m} \mid 0 \leq m\right\} \cup\left\{b^{n} \mid 0 \leq n\right\}$
questions.explanation: Detailed Video Solution , with Complete Analysis:  https://youtu.be/WqDkuKn20L4?t=1915&feature=shared Method 1: Note that Empty String $\epsilon$ is Not accepted by the given PDA, So options $B,C,D$ are eliminated. Empty String $\epsilon$ is Not accepted because from initial state, on empty tape, we cannot empty our stack since stack bottom symbol $\bot$ can be removed only in state $q$ But on empty tape, we can not reach to state $q$ from state $s.$ Method 2: Note that to empty our stack, the stack bottom symbol $\bot$ can be removed only in state $q.$ To reach state $q$, from $s$ or from $p,$ we need symbol $A$ on Top-of-the-stack (TOS). Symbol $A$ is pushed in the stack by symbol $a$ in the input string. So, our input string must have at least one $a.$  In the initial state $s$, for every $a$ in the input string, we push one $A$ in the stack. The complement of the language L, that is, $\sum^* – \text{ L}$ is denoted by $L’$. Which of the following is true? (a) Both $L$ and $L’$ are regular languages. (b) $L$ is a context-free language and $L’$ is a regular language. (c) Both $L$ and $L’$ are context-free languages. (d) $L$ is a context-free language and $L’$ is not a context-free language.  (e) Neither is $L$ a context-free language nor is $L’$ a context-free language.

questions.explanation: (a,b)* is actually you have written in “ easier to write for self understanding “ notation type way of representing “reg Language “ in which comma is understood as union ,although it is generally not seen in ToC and programming . A “union” can be represented using square brackets “[]”  like [a-z] or using  $\cup$ or using “+”  like (a+b) , according to the use and the convention. in regex, whereas “,” is just a comma [a-z] a very famous regex (programming) , means at-least 1 literal from “a or b or or ….z” ,which is quite similar to (a+b+...+z) in ToC A reg language can be represented in Grammar form or DFA or NFA or e-NFA or in Regex . Now in terms of ToC,  (a+b)* means any number of times either a or b or nothing :  $\epsilon$ , a , aa… , aaa...b  ,  b , bb , bbb …… , bbb…..a , ab ,ba , aa..b… , b...aa…. , likewise (a*b*)* means any number of times a , followed by any number of times b  : a , aa… , aaa...b  ,  b , bb , bbb …… , bbb….

Consider the language given below:

L={P!=w | P is prefix of w and w <-{0,1}*}

C.L is CSL    CORRECT ANSWER

questions.explanation: It’s not regular we can not write regular expressions for it. Stack logic we can not use because if we push all the characters of ‘ p ’ then we can not compare the first character of  p  with the first character of  ‘w ’  as the first character of p will be at the bottom of the stack. So, it’s not a Context Free Language. L is Context-Sensitive Language. If you can write a program to solve this problem(to accept this language) then it's Context-Sensitive Language as long as the space complexity is linear. Now we can easily write a program to do this. Code Hint: Start comparing w and p from the beginning and if till the last character of p all the character matches then the string belongs to your language. raja11sep answered Dec 21, 2022 • edited Dec 21, 2022 by raja11sep raja11sep comment Share Follow See all 2 Comments 2 2 Comments reply gatecse commented Dec 21, 2022 reply Follow flag That’s true. questions.questionText: A context-free grammar is in Chomsky Normal Form if every rule is of the form \[ \begin{array}{l} A \longrightarrow B C \\ A \longrightarrow a \end{array} \] where $a$ is a terminal, $A, B$ and $C$ are variables except $B$ and $C$ cannot be start variables. We only permit rule $S \longrightarrow \varepsilon$ if $S$ is a start variable. Given the following grammar, convert it to Chomsky Normal Form. \[ \begin{array}{l} S \longrightarrow A S B \mid a B \\ A \longrightarrow B \mid S \\ B \longrightarrow b \mid \varepsilon \end{array} \]
questions.questionHtml:
A context-free grammar is in Chomsky Normal Form if every rule is of the form
\[
\begin{array}{l}
A \longrightarrow B C \\
A \longrightarrow a
\end{array}
\]
where $a$ is a terminal, $A, B$ and $C$ are variables except $B$ and $C$ cannot be start variables. We only permit rule $S \longrightarrow \varepsilon$ if $S$ is a start variable.

Given the following grammar, convert it to Chomsky Normal Form.
\[
\begin{array}{l}
S \longrightarrow A S B \mid a B \\
A \longrightarrow B \mid S \\
B \longrightarrow b \mid \varepsilon
\end{array}
\]

questions.questionText: What does right quotient actually mean???? Which of the following is incorrect? (/ is right quotient) A If $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are CFL, then $L_{1} / L_{2}$ is regular. Correct Option Solution : (a) Regular, CFL, and recursive languages are closed under right quotient. B If $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are regular, then $L_{1} / L_{2}$ is regular. C If $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are RE, then $L_{1} / L_{2}$ is RE. D If $L_{1}$ is CFL and $L_{2}$ is regular then $L_{1} / L_{2}$ is CFL.
questions.questionHtml:
What does right quotient actually mean????

Which of the following is incorrect? (/ is right quotient)

A If $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are CFL, then $L_{1} / L_{2}$ is regular.
Correct Option

Solution :
(a)

Regular, CFL, and recursive languages are closed under right quotient.

B If $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are regular, then $L_{1} / L_{2}$ is regular.

C If $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are RE, then $L_{1} / L_{2}$ is RE.

D If $L_{1}$ is CFL and $L_{2}$ is regular then $L_{1} / L_{2}$ is CFL.

questions.questionHtml:
Number of 3 state DFA with designated initial state can be constructed over the alphabet 

$\sum$ = {0,1,2} with exactly 2 final states is

  1. $3^{8}$ B)$3^{9}$  C) $3^{10}$   D) $3^{11}$

Answer is C
questions.explanation: My reasoning for this question is: As we have a $DFA$ having $3$ states with exactly two as the final states. so to select $2$ final states from $3$ states we can select it in $^{3}\textrm{C}_{2}$ ways  so now we have $3$ $DFA’s$ The alphabet given in the question contains $3$ symbols  $({0,1,2})$ $(each$ $symbol$ $from$ $each$ $state$ $has$ $3$ $choices$ $either$ $it$ $can$ $loop$ $over$ $the$ $same$ $state$, $or$ $go$ $to$ $any$ $one$ $state$ $from$ $the$ $remaining$ $two$) And , as it is a $DFA$ every state should have transitions for all the symbols and hence for $3$ states each having $3$ symbols . (For forming a valid String we are only taking transition on one symbol per state). thus the choices we have for all the $3$ states and $3$ symbols will be $3^9$ and initially we had $^{3}\textrm{C}_{2}$ for selecting the final states thus total $DFA’s$ possible  $3^9*3$ $3^{10}$   Pranavpurkar answered Oct 30, 2022 Pranavpurkar co

For DFA we have to give transition for every input alphabet at every state. like an example of DFA for exactly two b’s, so in this DFA there will a dead state which will trap all the strings having greater than two b’s. questions.questionText: Assume that $f(n)$ and $g(n)$ are asymptotically positive. Which of the following is correct? $f(n)=O(g(n))$ and $g(n)=O(h(n)) \Rightarrow f(n)=\omega(h(n))$ $f(n)=\Omega(g(n))$ and $g(n)=\Omega(h(n)) \Rightarrow f(n)=O(h(n))$ $f(n)=o(g(n))$ and $g(n)=o(h(n)) \Rightarrow f(n)=o(h(n))$ $f(n)=\omega(g(n))$ and $g(n)=\omega(h(n)) \Rightarrow f(n)=\Omega(h(n))$
questions.questionHtml:
Assume that $f(n)$ and $g(n)$ are asymptotically positive. Which of the following is correct?

  1. $f(n)=O(g(n))$ and $g(n)=O(h(n)) \Rightarrow f(n)=\omega(h(n))$
  2. $f(n)=\Omega(g(n))$ and $g(n)=\Omega(h(n)) \Rightarrow f(n)=O(h(n))$
  3. $f(n)=o(g(n))$ and $g(n)=o(h(n)) \Rightarrow f(n)=o(h(n))$
  4. $f(n)=\omega(g(n))$ and $g(n)=\omega(h(n)) \Rightarrow f(n)=\Omega(h(n))$
questions.explanation: The notation Ω(n) is the formal way to express the lower bound of an algorithm's running time. It measures the best case time complexity or the best amount of time an algorithm can possibly take to complete. For example, for a function f(n) Ω(f(n)) ≥ { g(n) : there exists c > 0 and n0 such that g(n) ≤ c.f(n) for all n > n0. } According to Transitive Property f(n) = o(g(n)) and g(n) = o(h(n)) ⇒ f(n) = o(h(n)) is Correct

questions.questionText: Match List I with List II : List I List II (A) Type $0$ (I) Finite automata (B) Type $1$ (II) Tuning machine (C) Type $2$ (III) Linear bound automata (D) Type $3$ (IV) Pushdown automata Choose the correct answer from the options given below : $(\text{A})-\text{(III)}, (\text{B})-(\text{IV}), (\text{C})-(\text{II}), (\text{D})-(\text{I})$ $(\text{A})-(\text{II}), (\text{B})-(\text{III}), (\text{C})-(\text{IV}), (\text{D})-(\text{I})$ $(\text{A})-(\text{III}), (\text{B})-(\text{IV}), (\text{C})-(\text{I}), (\text{D})-(\text{II})$ $(\text{A})-(\text{II}), (\text{B})-(\text{III}), (\text{C})-(\text{II}), (\text{D})-(\text{IV})$
questions.questionHtml:
Match List I with List II :

List I List II
(A) Type $0$ (I) Finite automata
(B) Type $1$ (II) Tuning machine
(C) Type $2$ (III) Linear bound automata
(D) Type $3$ (IV) Pushdown automata

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :

  1. $(\text{A})-\text{(III)}, (\text{B})-(\text{IV}), (\text{C})-(\text{II}), (\text{D})-(\text{I})$
  2. $(\text{A})-(\text{II}), (\text{B})-(\text{III}), (\text{C})-(\text{IV}), (\text{D})-(\text{I})$
  3. $(\text{A})-(\text{III}), (\text{B})-(\text{IV}), (\text{C})-(\text{I}), (\text{D})-(\text{II})$
  4. $(\text{A})-(\text{II}), (\text{B})-(\text{III}), (\text{C})-(\text{II}), (\text{D})-(\text{IV})$
questions.explanation: According to the Chomsky Hierarchy : Type $0$ grammar is unrestricted grammar which is accepted by the turning machine. Type $1$ grammar is the context-sensitive grammar that is accepted by linear bounded automata. Type $2$ grammar is context-free grammar which is accepted by push-down automata Type $3$ grammar is regular grammar which is accepted by finite automata. So $A=(II),B=(III),C=(IV),D=(I)$   Hira Thakur answered Nov 5, 2022 Hira Thakur comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes Machine equivalent to Type 0 Grammer is Turing Machine. Machine Equivalent to type 1 Grammer(CSL) is Linear bounded automata. Machine Equivalent to Type 2 Grammer( CFL) is PUSH DOWN AUTOMATA. Type 3 Grammer is regular Grammer and equivalent system is Finite automata.   Hence Option B. supreetshukla answered Nov 15, 2022 supreetshukla comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.explanation: As we know that $(r)^*=\epsilon,r,rr,rrr,rrrr...\infty$,$0$ or more occurrence of r. For eg: $(ab)^*$ can generate $0$ or more occurrence of string $ab$. This regular expression can generate following strings:$(\epsilon,ab,abab,ababab....)$ In the same way $(ab^*)^*=(\epsilon,ab^*,ab^*ab^*,ab^*ab^*ab^*…...)$,which can also be written as:  $(ab^*)^*=(\epsilon,a,ab,abb…,aa,aba,aab,abba,abab,ababb….)\equiv(\epsilon+a(a+b)^*)$ Now another regular expression $(a+ab^*b)^*$ can be written as: $(a+ab^*b)^*=(a(\epsilon+b^*b)^*)\rightarrow(a(\epsilon+b^+))^*\rightarrow(a(\epsilon+b,bb,bbb,bbbb….))^*\rightarrow (a,ab,abb,abbb,abbbb….)^*\equiv(ab^*)^*$ $\therefore (ab^*)^*\equiv (a+ab^*b)^*$ both the regular expression generate the same sets of strings.   Hira Thakur answered Sep 16, 2022 Hira Thakur comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 2 2 votes S1: (a+ab*b)* S2 = (ab*)* = (a+ab*)* = (a+ab*b)* Any strings with any number of a’s consecutively in S2 wi

questions.questionText: Let $n$ be a positive integer, and let $V=\{f \in \mathbb{R}[x] \mid \operatorname{deg} f \leq n\}$ be the real vector space of real polynomials of degree at most $n$. Let $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{R}}(V)$ denote the real vector space of linear transformations from $V$ to itself. For $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, let $T_{m} \in \text{End}_{\mathbb{R}}(V)$ be such that $\left(T_{m} f\right)(x)=f(x+m)$ for all $f \in V$. Then the dimension of the vector subspace of $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{R}}(V)$ given by $$\operatorname{Span}\left(\left\{T_{m} \mid m \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\right)$$ is $1$ $n$ $n+1$ $n^{2}$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $n$ be a positive integer, and let $V=\{f \in \mathbb{R}[x] \mid \operatorname{deg} f \leq n\}$ be the real vector space of real polynomials of degree at most $n$. For $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, let $T_{m} \in \text{End}_{\mathbb{R}}(V)$ be such that $\left(T_{m} f\right)(x)=f(x+m)$ for all $f \in V$. questions.questionText: Consider polynomials \[ f_{1}(x, y)=\sum_{i, j=0}^{\infty} a_{i j} x^{i} y^{j} \quad \text { and } \quad f_{2}(x, y)=\sum_{i, j=0}^{\infty} b_{i j} x^{i} y^{j} \in \mathbb{R}[x, y] \] $($where $a_{i j}=b_{i j}=0$ for all but finitely many $(i, j) \in \mathbb{N}^{2} ),$ such that $f_{1}(p, q)=f_{2}(p, q)$ for all $(p, q) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ satisfying $p^{2}=q^{2}$. Which of the following sentences is true for all such $f_{1}$ and $f_{2}?$  $a_{00}=b_{00}$, but we may not have $a_{i j}=b_{i j}$ for all $(i, j)$ with $i+j=1$. $a_{i j}=b_{i j}$ if $i+j \leq 1$, but we may not have $a_{i j}=b_{i j}$ for all $(i, j)$ with $i+j=2$. $a_{i j}=b_{i j}$ if $i+j \leq 2$, but we may not have $a_{i j}=b_{i j}$ for all $(i, j)$ with $i+j=3$. $a_{i j}=b_{i j}$ if $i+j \leq 3$, but we may not have $f_{1}=f_{2}$.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider polynomials
\[ f_{1}(x, y)=\sum_{i, j=0}^{\infty} a_{i j} x^{i} y^{j} \quad \text { and } \quad f_{2}(x, y)=\sum_{i, j=0}^{\infty} b_{i j} x^{i} y^{j} \in \mathbb{R}[x, y] \]
$($where $a_{i j}=b_{i j}=0$ for all but finitely many $(i, j) \in \mathbb{N}^{2} ),$ such that $f_{1}(p, q)=f_{2}(p, q)$ for all $(p, q) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ satisfying $p^{2}=q^{2}$. Which of the following sentences is true for all such $f_{1}$ and $f_{2}?$ 

  1. $a_{00}=b_{00}$, but we may not have $a_{i j}=b_{i j}$ for all $(i, j)$ with $i+j=1$.
  2. $a_{i j}=b_{i j}$ if $i+j \leq 1$, but we may not have $a_{i j}=b_{i j}$ for all $(i, j)$ with $i+j=2$.
  3. $a_{i j}=b_{i j}$ if $i+j \leq 2$, but we may not have $a_{i j}=b_{i j}$ for all $(i, j)$ with $i+j=3$.
  4. $a_{i j}=b_{i j}$ if $i+j \leq 3$, but we may not have $f_{1}=f_{2}$.

options.label: B

questions.questionText: Doubt 1: CFL $\cap$ DCFL = CFL  CFL – Context Free Languages DCFL – Deterministic Context Free Languages Can you prove above expression   Doubt 2: Consider L$_{1}$ = Language generated by a machine M1 L$_{2}$ = Language generated by a machine M2 Machine can be – FA, PDA, LBA, or TM Assuming Machine M2 is more powerful than M1  Let L$_{3}$ = L$_{1}$  $\cap$  L$_{2}$ Now can we say that  L$_{3}$ can be generated by Machine M2 For eg: L1 =  Context Free Language (i.e Generated by NPDA) L2 =  Recursively enumerable language (i.e Generated by TM) Now can we say   L$_{1}$  $\cap$  L$_{2}$  is Recursively Enumerable Language i.e it can be generated by a TM   Doubt 3: Non Recursively Enumerable Language $\cap$ Any language = Non Recursively Enumerable Language Is this statement correct/always true?
questions.questionHtml:
Doubt 1:

CFL $\cap$ DCFL = CFL 

CFL – Context Free Languages

DCFL – Deterministic Context Free Languages

Can you prove above expression

 

Doubt 2:

Consider L$_{1}$ = Language generated by a machine M1

L$_{2}$ = Language generated by a machine M2

Machine can be – FA, PDA, LBA, or TM

Assuming Machine M2 is more powerful than M1 

Let L$_{3}$ = L$_{1}$  $\cap$  L$_{2}$

Now can we say that  L$_{3}$ can be generated by Machine M2

For eg:

L1 = Context Free Language (i.e Generated by NPDA)

L2 = Recursively enumerable language (i.e Generated by TM)

Now can we say  L$_{1}$  $\cap$  L$_{2}$ is Recursively Enumerable Language i.e it can be generated by a TM

 

Doubt 3:

Non Recursively Enumerable Language $\cap$ Any language = Non Recursively Enumerable Language

Is this statement correct/always true?

questions.explanation: if length of each string is finite lets say N, we can enumerate it with sets of natural numbers, you can enumerate by beginning with N boxes, fill the first box with 2 possiblities, 0 or 1. second box with 2 more possibilities so 2x2. and so on. so they are countable and finite as well. in this case there are 2x2x2...2 = 2^N strings possible, at the last box, you will exhaust all the possiblities, and cover all possible strings. meas it is finite. this is only possible if length is finite. but if length of each string is itself infinite, we cant count it. it follows from Cantor’s diagonal argument. If you arrange all the strings as per their digit, there is always one more infinite string that is different from all other strings, you can always form it so that it differs from string1 in 1 st  bit, from string2 in 2 nd  bit and so on. that is uncountable set. Assuming such a run is chosen randomly, what is the fraction of times that the state $s_2$ is expected to appear in the run? $\frac{1}{7}$ $\frac{2}{7}$ $\frac{3}{7}$ $\frac{5}{7}$ None of the above

Assuming such a run is chosen randomly, what is the fraction of times that the state $s_2$ is expected to appear in the run?

questions.explanation: From s₁: P(s₁→s₂) = 2/3, P(s₁→s₃) = 1/3 From s₂: P(s₂→s₁) = 1 From s₃: P(s₃→s₂) = 1 π₁,π₂,π₃ are probability of ending up in s₁,s₂s₃ π₁ = π₂(1) + π₃(0) [probability of ending up in s₁] π₂ = π₁(2/3) + π₃(1) [probability of ending up in s₂] π₃ = π₁(1/3) + π₂(0) [probability of ending up in s₃] π₁ + π₂ + π₃ = 1 [sum of probabilities = 1] by solving above equation we get π₁ = 3/7 π₂ = 3/7 π₃ = 1/7 Anmol VG answered Nov 23, 2024 Anmol VG comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes According to me, Fraction of times that the state S2 is expected to appear in the run= 1-(S2 never appears in the run) S2 never appears in the run is only possible when S1→ S3 only and else S2 will be in every run. 1-(1/3)=2/3 Hence E should be correct. Please do mention if I’m wrong.
